clinicalPearls: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity each occurs in more than 80% of adults with acute bacterial meningitis, but the complete triad is frequently absent; a depressed level of consciousness is seen in over 75% (Harrison 22e p.1119).
Acute presentation can be either fulminant over hours or subacute over several days; nausea, vomiting, and photophobia are common (Harrison 22e p.1119).

Nuchal rigidity is the pathognomonic sign of meningeal irritation; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are classic but of uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in the very young, elderly, immunocompromised, or obtunded (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120).

S. pneumoniae (~50%) and N. meningitidis (~25%) are the leading causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis; group B streptococci (~15%) and L. monocytogenes (~10%) follow, with H. influenzae type b now <10% (Harrison 22e p.1118).

Petechial or purpuric skin lesions are an important clue to meningococcal infection; the rash starts as a maculopapular eruption resembling a viral exanthem then becomes petechial on trunk, extremities, mucosae, conjunctivae, and sometimes palms/soles (Harrison 22e p.1118, p.1120).

Listeria meningitis should be considered in neonates, pregnant women, those over 60, and immunocompromised hosts; infection is acquired from contaminated foods such as soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, deli meats, and uncooked hotdogs (Harrison 22e p.1119).

Seizures occur in 15-40% of bacterial meningitis cases; focal seizures suggest focal ischemia/infarction, cortical venous thrombosis with hemorrhage, or focal edema, while generalized seizures may reflect hyponatremia or cerebral anoxia (Harrison 22e p.1120).
More than 90% of bacterial meningitis patients have a CSF opening pressure above 180 mmH2O, and 20% exceed 400 mmH2O; raised ICP is the major cause of obtundation/coma (Harrison 22e p.1120).

Viral meningitis is distinguished from encephalitis by the absence of stupor, coma, marked confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic signs; their presence points toward encephalitis or another process (Harrison 22e p.1123).
Profound CNS depression, seizures, or focal deficits should never be attributed to uncomplicated viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123).

A lymphocytic pleocytosis combined with a low CSF glucose should raise suspicion for fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningitis or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis rather than typical viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1124).

Neurologic injury in bacterial meningitis can progress even after CSF sterilization because much of the damage stems from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial injury (Harrison 22e p.1119).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that may cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised ICP, and stroke, with meninges, subarachnoid space, and parenchyma often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) colonize the nasopharynx, cross or bypass epithelial tight junctions to enter the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement via a polysaccharide capsule, then reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. Bacteria multiply readily in CSF given its scarce leukocytes, complement, and immunoglobulin, which impair opsonization. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (LPS of gram-negatives, teichoic acid and peptidoglycan of pneumococci) that drive microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, and endothelium to produce TNF-alpha and IL-1 beta; these cytokines synergistically increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema, protein leakage), and the proteinaceous leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and arachnoid resorption causing hydrocephalus and interstitial edema. Leukocyte adhesion and degranulation, excitatory amino acids, and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, basal arterial narrowing/vasculitis with thrombosis, and venous/sinus thrombosis cause ischemia and infarction; combined interstitial, vasogenic, and cytotoxic edema raise ICP and may produce herniation (Harrison 22e p.1118-1120). Viral (aseptic) meningitis produces meningeal irritation with a CSF inflammatory profile but, by definition, does not produce the parenchymal dysfunction of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1123).
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex virus encephalitis (HSV-1) and other viral meningoencephalitides (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Rickettsial disease, notably Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii), and ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Focal suppurative CNS infections: subdural or epidural empyema and brain abscess (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Subarachnoid hemorrhage (the major noninfectious consideration) and pituitary apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.1121-1122)
Subacute meningitis from M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis, and Treponema pallidum (Harrison 22e p.1122)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae CNS infection, which can mimic viral meningitis/encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1124)
infectionMimics: HSV encephalitis presenting with headache, fever, altered consciousness, focal deficits, and seizures (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Rocky Mountain spotted fever with high fever, headache, and a rash evolving from maculopapular to petechial/purpuric, easily confused with meningococcemia (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis with fever, headache, confusion, and leukopenia/thrombocytopenia with elevated transaminases (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Untreated or partially treated bacterial meningitis mimicking aseptic meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123)
Early fungal, mycobacterial, or syphilitic (T. pallidum) meningitis with lymphocytic pleocytosis and not-yet-low glucose (Harrison 22e p.1123)
Meningitis due to Mycoplasma, Listeria, Brucella, Coxiella, Leptospira, and Rickettsia species (Harrison 22e p.1123)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chemical meningitis from rupture of tumor contents (cystic glioma, craniopharyngioma, epidermoid or dermoid cyst) into CSF (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Inflammatory disorders: sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1121-1122)
Uveomeningitic syndromes including Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and pituitary apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.1122)
additionalInvestigations: CSF examination is the diagnostic cornerstone; classic bacterial findings are PMN pleocytosis >100/uL (90%), low glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL) and/or CSF/serum glucose ratio <0.4 (~60%), elevated protein >0.45 g/L (90%), and raised opening pressure >180 mmH2O (90%) (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)
CSF Gram stain positive in >60% and bacterial culture positive in >70-80%; culture remains required for susceptibility testing (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)
Blood cultures should be obtained immediately when bacterial meningitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1120)

CSF multiplex PCR (e.g., FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel) detects S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, L. monocytogenes, H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, plus HSV-1/2, enteroviruses, VZV, HHV-6, and parechovirus, but does not replace culture (Harrison 22e p.1121, p.1124)

Neuroimaging before LP (CT or MRI) when immunocompromised, recent head trauma, depressed consciousness, papilledema, or focal deficits; MRI preferred for edema/ischemia and shows diffuse meningeal enhancement after gadolinium (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)

For suspected viral meningitis: CBC with differential, liver and renal function, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase; CSF PCR is the diagnostic procedure of choice for enteroviral and HSV CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.1124)
Biopsy of petechial skin lesions may reveal organisms on Gram stain in meningococcemia (Harrison 22e p.1121)
redFlags: Petechial or purpuric rash suggesting meningococcemia, which can be fulminant and fatal within hours of symptom onset (Harrison 22e p.1118)

Deteriorating consciousness, papilledema, dilated poorly reactive pupils, sixth nerve palsy, decerebrate posturing, or the Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations) indicating raised ICP (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Cerebral herniation, the most disastrous complication of raised ICP, reported in 1-8% of bacterial meningitis cases (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Focal neurologic findings, which mandate prompt MRI to detect focal suppurative infection (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Seizures or status epilepticus at presentation (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Stupor, coma, or marked confusion in a presumed viral meningitis, which instead suggest encephalitis or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1123)
harrison.prognosis: Mortality from bacterial meningitis varies by organism: about 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, or group B streptococci; ~15% for L. monocytogenes; and ~20% for S. pneumoniae. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age in infancy or over 50, comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delayed treatment; very low CSF glucose (<2.2 mmol/L) and very high CSF protein (>3 g/L) also predict worse outcomes. Moderate-to-severe sequelae occur in roughly 25% of survivors, including impaired intellect, memory loss, seizures, hearing loss, dizziness, and gait disturbance. In adults, recovery from viral meningitis is excellent, with only rare lingering headache, mild cognitive complaints, or asthenia; outcomes in infants/neonates under 1 year are less certain, with reported intellectual impairment, learning disability, and hearing loss (Harrison 22e p.1123, p.1125).
pitfalls: Awaiting LP or neuroimaging to start therapy: blood cultures and empirical treatment must not be delayed in suspected bacterial meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Assuming antibiotics given a few hours before LP invalidate the CSF; they do not significantly alter WBC count or glucose, nor reliably prevent Gram stain or PCR detection (Harrison 22e p.1120)
Relying on multiplex PCR alone: it omits S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and many gram-negatives, and cannot provide susceptibility data (Harrison 22e p.1121)
Interpreting meningeal enhancement on MRI as diagnostic of meningitis; it occurs in any condition with increased blood-brain barrier permeability (Harrison 22e p.1121)

Overreliance on Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, which have uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in vulnerable groups; cervical spine disease in the elderly can cause false-positive nuchal rigidity (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120)

Misreading an early PMN pleocytosis in viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps) as bacterial; a PMN-predominant CSF without a diagnosis should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (Harrison 22e p.1123-1124)
Forgetting that giving IV 50% glucose before LP can take hours to alter CSF glucose, so it rarely confounds early sampling (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121)
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal grading scale is given for acute meningitis; instead Harrison enumerates prognostic risk factors for death in bacterial meningitis (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, raised ICP, age <1 or >50, shock or need for ventilation, treatment delay, CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L, CSF protein >3 g/L). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis, a prospectively validated bacterial meningitis score yields a negative predictive value of about 99.7% in children, and CSF protein >0.5 g/L and serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL favor bacterial over aseptic meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123-1125).
management: Immediate empirical intravenous third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime without waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging
Add vancomycin to cover penicillin-resistant pneumococcus and amoxicillin to cover Listeria in neonates, older, pregnant, or immunocompromised patients
Adjunctive dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose, particularly for suspected pneumococcal disease
Narrow antimicrobial therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known
Supportive management of raised intracranial pressure, seizures, and fluid balance, with intensive care for depressed consciousness or shock
Monitor and manage complications including hydrocephalus, seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss
Notify public health, give chemoprophylaxis with rifampicin or ciprofloxacin to close meningococcal contacts, and reinforce vaccination
